text: {"answer": "The evidence is mixed, with several trials and meta-analyses supporting intermittent fasting for weight loss while other reviews find it no better than standard dieting. Supporting studies include a trial in obese women where intermittent fasting combined with calorie restriction produced greater weight loss than the food-based version [23334c40ad6b#1], and a 12-week high-protein intermittent-fasting intervention in obese adults that was reported as effective for weight loss [c74e11d8769a#0]. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found intermittent energy restriction produced weight loss comparable to continuous restriction in its reported outcomes [e5aee0e45fc5#0], and a pilot study found alternate-day fasting equally effective as daily restriction [d5b094e9e37f#7]. The contradicting side is substantial: a major Cochrane review of 22 trials with nearly 2,000 adults found intermittent fasting did not produce significantly more weight loss than standard diet advice [5a896703f2e3#0]. Harvard's Nutrition Source notes that research does not consistently show intermittent fasting is superior to continuous low-calorie diets [44e3472ec92d#2], and a 100-person one-year trial found no advantage over daily restriction [44e3472ec92d#7]. One meta-analysis reported a small significant weight advantage for intermittent fasting [f5eeafdf6fc3#1]. Overall, it appears roughly comparable to continuous calorie restriction rather than clearly superior.", "confidence": 62, "one_line": "Intermittent fasting produces weight loss similar to continuous calorie restriction, though a major Cochrane review found no significant extra benefit over standard dieting."}
